what.definition: An AI Agent is an autonomous goal-directed software system that uses LLMs to perceive environment state, reason over goals, select tools, and execute multi-step workflows.
what.summary: Comprehensive conceptual and interactive guide to building stateful, resilient AI agent systems.

why.impact: Agentic architectures introduce dynamic policy execution, self-evaluation, and deterministic failure recovery.
why.summary: Single-prompt LLM wrappers break when tasked with complex multi-step enterprise workflows requiring memory and tool selection.

terms.detailedDefinition: Visual hierarchy guides the user's eyes through an interface. Instead of specifying hardcoded fonts, instruct the AI to analyze element importance first and ask clarification questions to align on size scaling, weight contrast, and visual density.
terms.shortDefinition: Arranging UI elements in order of visual importance using scale, contrast, and weight.
terms.whyItMatters: If you instruct an AI vaguely, it defaults to a uniform, boring structure. Prompting the AI to think about hierarchy and ask for clarification forces it to design with distinct focal points rather than generic, monotonous text blocks.

terms.detailedDefinition: Negative space is an active design tool that organizes content without physical borders. Ask the AI to plan a spacing hierarchy (margins, padding, gaps) first, and ask back about the desired layout density.
terms.shortDefinition: The empty breathing room surrounding and between UI components that groups elements and enhances legibility.
terms.whyItMatters: AIs tend to default to conservative, tight spacing to save room. Asking the AI to analyze spacing and ask for your layout preferences prevents cluttered, claustrophobic designs and achieves clean, breathing breathing room.

terms.detailedDefinition: Accessible web design requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Ask the AI to evaluate color contrast mathematically and query you on strict accessibility compliance versus specific brand tint options.
terms.shortDefinition: The difference in light intensity between text/foreground elements and their background, ensuring maximum accessibility.
terms.whyItMatters: AIs often pair light gray text on light backgrounds to attempt a 'minimalist' look, violating readability standards. Instructing the AI to check contrast metrics first and ask for alignment ensures beautiful, readable, WCAG-friendly palettes.

terms.detailedDefinition: Interactive affordance makes buttons and inputs look clickable. Direct the AI to outline its planned interactive states (hover, focus, click transitions) first, and ask you to choose the tactile intensity of the feedback.
terms.shortDefinition: Visual signifiers that communicate how an element behaves and how users should interact with it.
terms.whyItMatters: Without prompting, AIs often render static, flat buttons that don't react to a cursor. Asking the AI to explain states and ask for alignment ensures buttons have clear interactive weight and satisfying feedback.

terms.detailedDefinition: Aesthetic consistency prevents visual chaos. Instruct the AI to design a mini design system (consistent corner radiuses, border weights, gap increments) and align with you on a styling motif.
terms.shortDefinition: Using standardized, repeating design variables (typography, spacing, borders) to create a unified design system.
terms.whyItMatters: Without a consistency constraint, an AI might mix random styles (like highly rounded cards with sharp buttons). Declaring a unified motif and asking for confirmation makes the output feel extremely cohesive.

terms.detailedDefinition: Responsive fluidity adapts layouts to any viewport. Ask the AI to plan grid or flex structures first and query you on the breakpoint behavior and max-width layout thresholds.
terms.shortDefinition: Designing layouts that fluidly adapt, scale, and reorganize across all screens and window dimensions.
terms.whyItMatters: If you specify static pixel dimensions, the AI compiles hardcoded CSS that breaks on mobile. Ordering the AI to analyze responsive reflow and ask for parameters guarantees a mobile-optimized, fluid layout.

terms.detailedDefinition: Type pairing combines an expressive, stylistic display face for headers with a neutral, highly readable font for body elements. Direct the AI to suggest pairing combinations and ask which one fits your brand.
terms.shortDefinition: Using contrasting but complementary font families for titles and body text to convey a specific aesthetic mood.
terms.whyItMatters: Without explicit directives, AIs fall back to generic system font stacks. Asking the AI to propose pairings and align on a visual mood adds immediate character and professional, editorial weight.

terms.detailedDefinition: Micro-interactions use quick, physical transitions to smooth out state changes. Direct the AI to outline its animation durations and transition curves first, and ask for your preference on animation playfulness.
terms.shortDefinition: Subtle, organic UI transitions and animations that guide attention and confirm state changes.
terms.whyItMatters: When visual states change instantly, the transition feels robotic and jarring. Specifying physics curves and asking for alignment ensures high-end, responsive micro-animations.

paragraphs: **Goal Intake** — The user submits a natural-language goal. The orchestrator parses intent, identifies required capabilities, and selects relevant tools from the registry.
**Context Retrieval** — The memory module performs a semantic search over stored embeddings to surface prior facts, tool outputs, or conversation history relevant to the current goal.
**Planning** — The planner prompts the LLM with the goal plus retrieved context. The LLM returns an ordered action plan — either as structured JSON or a chain-of-thought trace.
**Tool Execution** — The tool router dispatches each planned action to the executor. Tools include web search, code sandboxes, browser control, file I/O, and external APIs.

**Evaluation & Loop** — The evaluator checks whether the execution result satisfies the success criteria. If not, it feeds failure context back to the orchestrator and triggers a new planning iteration.
**Response Delivery** — Once the evaluator confirms success, the final artefact (answer, code diff, report) is formatted and returned to the user. Results are optionally persisted to memory.

categories.analogy: Like a software engineering manager delegating backend, frontend, and QA tasks to developers.
categories.description: A central manager agent (orchestrator) decomposes goals, delegates tasks to specialized worker agents, collects results, and synthesizes the final output.
categories.details: Ideal for complex, multi-step workflows requiring strict quality control, consensus, or routing.
categories.primaryFocus: Task decomposition, delegation, and output synthesis
categories.subtitle: Orchestrator-Workers
categories.title: Hierarchical Orchestration

categories.analogy: Like a researcher who takes notes, bookmarks references, and builds a personal knowledge base over years.
categories.description: The agent stores and retrieves information across interactions, maintaining context through vector embeddings, conversation history, and external knowledge bases.
categories.details: Memory systems include short-term (working memory within a session), long-term (persisted across sessions via embeddings), and external memory (RAG over documents).
categories.primaryFocus: Context retention, retrieval, and working memory management
categories.subtitle: State Management
categories.title: Memory & Context

categories.analogy: A brainstorming session among design peers sharing ideas, voting, and converging on a solution.
categories.description: Independent agents interact directly, negotiate, and collaborate to solve a problem without a centralized manager.
categories.details: Useful for negotiation, multi-perspective debates, or open-ended creative tasks.
categories.primaryFocus: Peer negotiation, debate, and consensus mechanisms
categories.subtitle: Decentralized Network
categories.title: Peer Collaboration

categories.analogy: Like a project manager breaking down an epic into sprint tasks and adjusting when blockers appear.
categories.description: The agent decomposes goals into actionable plans, reasons through chain-of-thought, and adapts strategies when encountering obstacles.
categories.details: Planning encompasses ReAct loops, tree-of-thought search, and self-refinement patterns.
categories.subtitle: Core Intelligence
categories.title: Reasoning & Planning

categories.analogy: A developer reviewing their own code before submitting a PR.
categories.description: The agent evaluates its own output against success criteria, identifies failures, and triggers re-planning or correction loops.
categories.details: Self-evaluation can be rule-based (checklist), LLM-based (self-critique), or hybrid (automated tests + LLM judgment).
categories.subtitle: Quality Assurance
categories.title: Self-Evaluation

categories.analogy: An assembly line in a factory where each worker installs a specific part of a car.
categories.description: Agents work in a pipeline, passing data sequentially. Each agent receives input from the previous step, performs its specialized task, and hands off to the next.
categories.details: Best for structured pipelines where steps are predictable (e.g. Code Gen -> Lint -> Test -> Fix).
categories.primaryFocus: Linear hand-offs and deterministic stage-gate processing
categories.subtitle: Chain of Agents
categories.title: Sequential Choreography

categories.analogy: A triage doctor in an emergency room routing patients to specialists based on their symptoms.
categories.description: A supervisor agent monitors shared state, routes tasks dynamically to appropriate workers based on the current state, and decides when the overall goal is achieved.
categories.details: Best for open-ended problem solving where the path to the solution is non-linear and depends on intermediate findings.
categories.subtitle: Dynamic Routing
categories.title: Supervisor Router

categories.analogy: Like a developer using CLI tools, IDE features, and version control to complete a task.
categories.description: The agent invokes external tools — APIs, code interpreters, web browsers, file systems — to extend its capabilities beyond pure text generation.
categories.details: Tool use transforms the agent from a passive text generator into an active agent that can modify its environment.
categories.primaryFocus: External tool invocation and result integration
categories.subtitle: Action Execution
categories.title: Tool Use

categories.analogy: Like a scientist who hypothesizes, runs an experiment, observes results, and revises the hypothesis.
categories.description: The agent alternates between reasoning (Thought) and taking action (Act), then observes the result (Observation) to inform the next reasoning step.
categories.details: Each cycle: the agent thinks about what to do, executes a tool call or generates text, reads the result, and decides the next step. This loop continues until the goal is achieved or a max iteration limit is reached.
categories.subtitle: Thought-Action-Observation Loop
categories.title: ReAct (Reason + Act)

categories.analogy: Like a project manager who writes a Gantt chart before the team starts working.
categories.description: The agent first creates a detailed step-by-step plan, then executes each step sequentially, checking off completion and adjusting as needed.
categories.details: Planning phase generates a structured list of subtasks with dependencies. Execution phase processes each subtask, marking completion. If a step fails, the agent can replan just that step without redoing the entire plan.
categories.subtitle: Separate Planning from Execution
categories.title: Plan-and-Execute

categories.analogy: Like dividing a book among multiple proofreaders, then compiling their notes into one edit list.
categories.description: The problem is decomposed into independent sub-problems, each solved by a separate agent instance in parallel, then results are combined by a reduce step.
categories.details: Map phase: the orchestrator splits the task and spawns parallel workers. Each worker solves its subtask independently. Reduce phase: a final aggregation step merges all results into a coherent answer.
categories.subtitle: Parallel Processing with Aggregation
categories.title: Map-Reduce Agent

categories.analogy: Like a chess player who reviews game replays to identify recurring tactical errors.
categories.description: The agent attempts a task, then reflects on what went wrong, stores lessons learned in a memory buffer, and uses those lessons to improve the next attempt.
categories.details: Unlike ReAct which observes immediate tool outputs, Reflexion maintains a persistent memory of past failures. Each retry incorporates the accumulated reflection log, allowing the agent to avoid repeating the same mistakes.
outOfScope: Tasks where failure is not informative
categories.primaryFocus: Learning from past failures across attempts
categories.subtitle: Self-Reflection with Memory
categories.title: Reflexion Agent

props.title: Choosing a Deployment Strategy

leaf.explanation: Dispatch independent tasks to parallel workers and aggregate results. Simple and highly scalable when tasks don't depend on each other.
A central orchestrator decomposes complex goals, delegates to specialized worker agents, and aggregates results. Best for workflows where tasks depend on each other.
tradeoffs: Orchestrator becomes a single point of failure
More agents to monitor and debug

leaf.explanation: For single-task agents without memory needs, a basic ReAct (Reason-Act) loop is sufficient. The agent observes, reasons, takes an action, and repeats.
leaf.recommendation: Use a simple single-agent ReAct loop.
tradeoffs: Easy to debug and reason about

leaf.explanation: For single-task agents that need persistent memory, add a vector store for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). This lets the agent recall relevant past interactions.
leaf.recommendation: Use a single-agent ReAct loop with vector store memory.

choices.rationale: Persistent memory enables learning from past interactions.
Stateless agents are easier to scale horizontally.
